presentation.title: Rotations
presentation.description: Rotational basics, 360 variations, back spot turn entries and exits. Build a foundation of rotational vocabulary.

This 360 variation uses more of a ballroom frame to create an elegant feel. It's a great option during the intro and verse of the song, especially if the energy of the music is slow, smooth or romantic.

presentation.description: Let's explore some new ways to enter the back spot turn using the concept of equivalent positions.
presentation.tips: In this lesson we use the change of place, back spot turn, reverse cross body and traveling turns.

pathSegments: Back Spot Turn Exit Inside Turn

presentation.description: This back spot turn exit is one of my favorites. It uses an overturn to change directions, creating a fun dynamic energy. Perfect for when the music is high energy.
presentation.tips: We use the inside turn in this lesson.
presentation.song: Échale Madera — DJ Ricky Campenelli ft. Jimmy Bosch

folders.name: Back Spot Turn Exit Leads Go Left
pathSegments: Back Spot Turn Exit Leads Go Left

presentation.description: We learned an exit where the follows turn left. Now let's learn an exit where the leads turn left on the second half.
presentation.song: Échale Madera — DJ Ricky Campenelli ft. Jimmy Bosch

folders.name: Back Spot Turn Exits Follows Go Left
pathSegments: Back Spot Turn Exits Follows Go Left

presentation.description: Now that we have some new ways to enter the back spot turn, let's explore some new ways to exit during the second half. You can also use these exits from a multiple back spot turn.
presentation.tips: In this lesson we use the back spot turn, reverse cross body and reverse inside turn.
presentation.song: Échale Madera — DJ Ricky Campenelli ft. Jimmy Bosch

presentation.description: The key frameworks leads and follows should be aware of: First half and second half, Follow is the focus (where is their weight?), 6 position diamond, Equivalent positions, 7 handholds + 3 levels.
Use these partner work exercises to improve your lead and follow fundamentals. Great as a warm-up or for focused fundamentals work.
presentation.tips: 0:08 — Follow the hand (frame) · 2:01 — Tension bridge · 3:20 — Arm position for turns · 4:49 — Torso connection · 6:02 — Blind following · 7:07 — Stay close to your partner

presentation.description: Let's learn how to rotate and reverse directions to create a nice dynamic in our dancing. We'll start by rotating on the spot and then use a more linear cross body lead.
presentation.tips: The back spot turn footwork will help in this lesson.

presentation.description: Salsa basics warmup for On1. Song: Ebbo — Sexteto Rumbahabana.
Salsa basics warmup for On2. Song: Ebbo — Sexteto Rumbahabana.

Daily practice turn drill for On2 timing.

Film a video social dancing together and play with the following: Use this week's moves, mix the entries and exits, interpret the music — use simple and smooth variations during the intro and verse, then increase the energy and dynamism in the montuno section.

presentation.description: In week 1 we'll be using the following moves from the Salsa Program. If you don't have access, no worries — these moves were listed as prerequisites, so you should know them already.

presentation.title: Back to Back
presentation.description: Cross body leads, turns, and barrel rolls — all while facing away from your partner.
Now let's learn the inside and outside turns facing away from your partner. The inside turn is a regular inside turn and the outside turn is a reverse outside turn.
presentation.tips: We'll use your knowledge of the inside turn and reverse outside turn in this lesson.

presentation.description: Now let's learn how to do the left turn while facing away from your partner.
presentation.tips: We use the left turn in this lesson.

presentation.description: In this lesson we're going back to back with the right turn and spot turn.
presentation.tips: Make sure you've practiced your spot turns.

folders.name: Back to Back Cross Body Leads
pathSegments: Back to Back Cross Body Leads

presentation.description: You've all done cross body leads before, but have you tried them while facing away from your partner?
presentation.tips: We'll use our knowledge of the cross body and reverse cross body for this lesson. Tip: to lead both of these back to back cross body leads the flick is on 5 (On1) or 2 (On2).

folders.name: Back to Back Right Turn & Spot Turn
pathSegments: Back to Back Right Turn & Spot Turn

presentation.description: In this lesson we're going back to back with the right turn and spot turn.
presentation.tips: Make sure you've practiced your spot turns.

presentation.description: You've all done double turns. Now, let's learn how to end a double turn with a barrel roll.
presentation.tips: We'll use the double turn in this lesson.

presentation.description: Let's go back to back with our inside and outside turns.
presentation.tips: We use the inside turn, outside turn, and reverse outside turn in this lesson.

presentation.description: For this week's challenge focus on two things: Interpret the music — match your moves to the energy of the song. Integrate everything you've learned in weeks 1 and 2 into a social dance.

presentation.title: Direction Changes
presentation.description: Checks, overturns, and reversals. Learn to change direction smoothly and dynamically.
Cross body lead reversal using check technique for direction changes.
For our first two direction changes we're going to use the outside turn.
presentation.tips: When dancing On1 the check happens on the 5. When dancing On2 the check happens on the 2.

presentation.description: The late check variation of the outside turn direction change.
presentation.tips: When dancing On1 the check is on the 7. When dancing On2 the check is on the 5.

presentation.description: This overturn goes left and happens on the fourth step of the cross body lead.
presentation.tips: When dancing On1 this overturn happens on the 5. When dancing On2 this overturn happens on the 2.

presentation.description: This overturn goes right and happens on the third step of the cross body lead.
presentation.tips: When dancing On1 this overturn happens on the 3. When dancing On2 this overturn happens on the 1.

presentation.description: The spot overturn technique for direction changes.
presentation.tips: We'll be using the Spot Turn in this lesson. Note: although the Spot Overturn looks like the Cape, it's more advanced and the timing is different.

presentation.description: Choose a slower song to start with. Checks and overturns are tricky when the music is fast! Practice executing your direction changes smoothly. Add in Week 1 and 2 material — rotations and back to back stuff — as you social dance.

presentation.title: Locks & Drops
presentation.description: Lock technique, drops, loops, and hair brushes across all turn types.
Inside turn with lock technique.
Left turn with lock technique.
Being successful with locks is all about technique. Stay close to your partner (forearm distance), relax your arms with elbows down, trace to maintain connection when you drop a hand.
presentation.tips: Vocabulary: a "lock" is when you keep holding on to the hand. A "drop" is when you drop the hand (also called a "hair brush" when over someone's head). A "loop" or "head loop" is another name for a common lock that goes around the head. Warmup exercise at 3:47 (explanation) and 9:47 (demo).

presentation.description: Combining all the different lock techniques you've learned across turn types.
Reverse outside turn with lock technique.
Right turn with lock technique.

This week's challenge is about combining all the different locks you just learned. As you social dance add in moves from previous weeks: Rotations (360s, spot turns with various entrances/exits), Back to back (back door turns, barrel turns), Direction changes (checks & overturns).

presentation.title: Hand Tosses
presentation.description: Toss connections, inside/outside tosses, and applying them in your social dancing.
Applying toss techniques in social dancing context.
presentation.tips: 0:14 What hand tosses are for + tips · 3:09 Toss to inside turn · 3:47 After a turn, toss from a lock · 5:53 After a turn, toss into a lock · 6:54 Lock with arm bounce · 9:17 Cross body options with right turn for lead · 11:28 Reverse cross body to wrap

folders.name: Applying Tosses In Your Dancing Part II
pathSegments: Applying Tosses In Your Dancing Part II

presentation.description: More toss applications in social dancing.
presentation.tips: 0:08 Toss to hammerlock from single hand turn · 2:30 Karate kid: toss toss block to hammerlock (right hand) · 5:21 Same starting with left hand · 6:30 Toss to back to back copa/outside turn

presentation.description: Cross body lead variations incorporating toss connections.
Inside tosses leading to lock and hammerlock positions.

Outside toss technique. Since hand toss movements go with the movement of your body, reviewing body movement is highly recommended. Great body movement makes your partner work smoother, more rhythmical and easier to follow.
Three great connection exercises to start with: Switching from a handhold to a wrist/toss connection, Karate kid (wax on) circles to the inside, Karate kid (wax off) circles to the outside.
presentation.tips: Try these exercises standing still first, then stepping in place to quick-quick-slow, and finally doing a basic. Improving your body movement (volume 2) will improve the rhythm of your hand tosses.

presentation.title: Bringing It All Together
presentation.description: Problem solving challenges: create your own variations using everything you've learned.
Use the 5 frameworks, weekly themes and your knowledge of basic moves to think of 4-6 copa variations. You can change the entrance, the amount of checks, the exit — whatever you like!
presentation.tips: The goal: explore, create and problem solve to solidify neural connections.

presentation.description: It's time to bring everything you know together and solve some problems! Combine all your tools — your experience, knowledge of basic moves, 5 frameworks, and weekly themes — and come up with 6-10 solutions for exiting a hammerlock.
presentation.tips: The goal: explore, create and problem solve to solidify neural connections. Don't watch the solutions video until you've tried ALL your assignments.

folders.name: Problem Solving Inside Turn With Check
pathSegments: Problem Solving Inside Turn With Check

presentation.description: Use the 5 frameworks, weekly themes and basic moves to think of AT LEAST 4-6 variations (or aim high with 10+). You can vary the entrance or the exit (handholds, positions etc.).
presentation.tips: You can do the inside turn with one check (the Wrap) or with two checks. The goal: explore, create and problem solve.

presentation.description: It's time to bring everything you've learned together and social dance! As an exercise, include as much as you've learned as possible while connecting to the music: Week 1 rotations, Week 2 back to back, Week 3 direction changes, Week 4 locks and drops, Week 5 hand tosses, Week 6 vary your exits for common positions.

Congratulations! Here are ideas for continuing your training: 1) Go through the program at least 3 more times. 2) Do the intermediate and advanced combos until you can execute each cleanly. 3) Modify combos by mixing them together or adding your own ideas. 4) Watch favorite dancers on YouTube/Instagram and deconstruct what they're doing. 5) Create your own moves using everything you've learned. 6) Practice BODY MOVEMENT daily — this is the magic of salsa.

lessons.title: 01 - Syncopation
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:45]** - **Initial Syncopation & Weight Transfer**: Adolfo introduces the first syncopated movement, a kick and twist on counts 8&1. Notice how the supporting leg maintains a soft knee to absorb the weight shift, while the core remains engaged to stabilize the upper body during the rapid foot articulation. The weight must transfer cleanly to allow the tapping motion on count 2.
- **[01:54]** - **Advanced Syncopated Rhythms (3&4&5)**: The sequence becomes more complex with an added "pa-di-ba-da" rhythm. This requires rapid, precise weight transfers from left to right, right to left, and left to right. The dancer must maintain a strong center and avoid over-committing weight to the extremities; keeping the axis vertically aligned over the balls of the feet is crucial for this speed.
- **[03:05]** - **Cha-Cha-Cha Syncopation Mechanics**: A new syncopation pattern is introduced on 8&1, 2&3, mimicking a cha-cha-cha rhythm. The footwork involves a kick, step forward, behind, open, and forward. The dancer must focus on grounding through the floor, using the inner thighs and core to control the momentum and cleanly hit the sharp, syncopated accents without losing balance.
- **[04:30]** - **Full Shine Sequence Breakdown**: During the slow run-through, observe the posture and isolation. The upper body remains relatively quiet, demonstrating excellent core engagement, while the lower body executes the intricate syncopations. This isolation ensures that the center of gravity remains stable, allowing for quick changes in direction and precise foot placement.
- **[05:46]** - **Shines to Music**: When executing the sequence to tempo, the importance of keeping the steps small and under the body becomes evident. Over-striding will pull the dancer off their axis, making the syncopations impossible to execute cleanly. The knees must act as shock absorbers, maintaining a grounded connection to the floor.
- **[08:10]** - **Initiating the "Trouble" Position**: The partner work begins with a cross body lead where the leader raises the right arm to create a crossed-arm ("trouble") hold on counts 2, 3. The leader must establish frame integrity early, using the lats rather than the shoulders to lift the arm, ensuring the follower receives a clear, grounded signal without compromising her posture.
- **[08:46]** - **Follower's Right Turn from Crossed Hold**: The leader initiates a right turn for the follower using the right arm. The follower must maintain a strong, active frame, offering slight resistance to the leader's connection. This allows the rotational force generated by the leader to transfer directly into the follower's core, facilitating a clean, balanced turn on her axis.
- **[09:05]** - **Hand Switch and Downward Compression**: The leader switches from a left-hand to right-hand hold and pushes down on count 5. This downward compression is crucial; it signals the follower to ground her weight and prepares her for the upcoming rotation. The leader must use body weight, not just arm strength, to create this compression, maintaining a solid frame.
- **[09:30]** - **Finger Rotation Mechanics**: During the turn on count 7, the leader must rotate his finger to allow the follower's hand to swivel smoothly. The follower must not grip tightly; instead, she maintains connection through a relaxed but toned hand, allowing the rotation to happen without creating torque on her wrist or shoulder.
- **[10:11]** - **Double Turn into Hammerlock**: The leader leads a double turn, transitioning into a hammerlock on the second rotation. This requires precise spatial awareness and distance management. The leader must keep the follower within her slot and maintain a consistent axis for her turns. The follower must engage her core to stay tight and balanced through the multiple rotations.
- **[10:34]** - **Exiting the Hammerlock**: On counts 5, 6, 7, the leader releases the left hand to exit the hammerlock. The timing of this release is critical; it must happen smoothly to allow the follower to unwind without losing momentum. The follower continues to travel down the line of dance, maintaining her frame integrity even as the connection changes.
- **[10:53]** - **Final Hand Switch**: The sequence finishes with a hand switch to the leader's left hand. This subtle change requires clear leader/follower mechanics. The leader must present the new hand connection distinctly, and the follower must be responsive, transitioning her frame without breaking the flow or losing her grounded connection.
- **[13:48]** - **Partner Work Execution**: When performed to music, the seamless integration of weight transfers, frame tone, and spatial awareness is paramount. The leader and follower must maintain constant communication through tension and compression, ensuring that each rotation, hand switch, and directional change is executed with precision and fluidity along the slot.

lessons.title: 02 - Syncopation Twist
lessons.rawSummary:
**[00:50]** - **Syncopated Weight Transfer**: Initiate the advanced footwork sequence by articulating precisely through the metatarsals during the rapid "8-and-1, 2-and-3" syncopations. You must maintain a lowered center of gravity to absorb these rapid, successive axis shifts without compromising your vertical alignment or allowing your weight to float.

**[01:48]** - **Rotational Core Mechanics (Twists)**: Execute the outward twist on count 2 and inward twist on count 3 by intensely isolating the hip joint and utilizing the obliques for rotational torque. Your standing leg must act as a rigid, grounded pillar, anchoring your center of mass while the free leg articulates the twist without disrupting your primary vertical axis.

**[04:02]** - **Directional Axis Shifts**: During the complex crossing sequence, manage your spatial footprint with strict precision. Ensure each crossover step involves a complete and deliberate commitment of your center of mass, utilizing the core to brake the lateral momentum and immediately redirect kinetic energy into the subsequent step.

**[08:02]** - **Frame Integrity & Grip Transitions**: Transitioning to the open hold requires immediate adaptation of your connection points. As you flip the palm up during the 5-6-7, establish a stable "pizza tray" connection that relies on upward structural resistance from your lats and core, rather than isolated arm strength, preparing the follower for upcoming rotational leads.

**[08:52]** - **Hammerlock Entry Mechanics**: To initiate the double turn into the hammerlock, the leader must generate clear rotational torque using the left hand connection while simultaneously managing their own spatial orientation. Pivot sharply on count 5, engaging your transverse abdominis to halt your own rotation cleanly, allowing you to secure the follower's right hand without collapsing the shared frame or closing the distance.

**[10:02]** - **Visual Leading & Spatial Redirection**: Exiting the hammerlock demands pristine spatial awareness and non-verbal communication. Present your hand clearly in the follower's direct visual field on count 1 to invite the crossover. This visual lead must be supported by a subtle weight shift in your own frame to clear the slot, dictating her new line of dance seamlessly.

**[11:51]** - **Compression and Reversal Forces**: As you bring the follower under the bridge, establish an immediate structural block on count 2. Absorb her forward momentum using your core and the connection point to create a localized zone of compression. Release this stored energy precisely on count 3 to sharply redirect her mass backward, manipulating her axis with controlled, elastic resistance.

**[15:52]** - **Grounding Mechanics in Heels**: For followers executing these sequences in heels, it is imperative to resist the biomechanical urge to elevate your center of mass. Drive your energy downward through the heel to brake your momentum and establish a deeply grounded connection to the floor. Utilize the entire articulation of the foot—rolling from toe to heel—to absorb kinetic impact and maintain a stable, lowered pelvic floor throughout rapid directional changes.

lessons.title: 03 - Jump the Rope
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:43]** - **Advanced Shine Footwork Initiation**: Begin breaking down the "Jump The Rope" shine. Ensure your weight transfers are crisp and stay on the balls of your feet. Engage your core to support the rapid directional changes while maintaining a grounded, athletic posture.
- **[01:05]** - **Vertical Level Changes & Core Engagement**: When executing the vertical level changes, utilize your quads and core to lower your center of gravity smoothly. Do not break or hinge at the waist. Maintaining your axis alignment here is critical for generating the power needed for the upward motion.
- **[02:25]** - **Syncopated Jumping Mechanics**: For the simultaneous tap and jump on counts 1 and 2, focus on precise lower body isolation. Your supporting leg must act as a spring; actively engage your ankle and calf to execute the micro-jump while your free foot taps lightly, controlling the split-second weight distribution.
- **[03:10]** - **Timing & Spatial Awareness**: As you move continuously through counts 4 and 5, maintain your spatial orientation within your slot. Despite the rapid rotational and linear footwork, your core stability and visual spotting must remain sharp to prevent drifting off your line.
- **[08:02]** - **Partnerwork Initiation & Frame Integrity**: Transition into the Cross Body Lead partnerwork. Leaders, initiate the movement from your center, maintaining a toned frame to clearly communicate the line of dance. Followers, receive this compression and ground through your standing leg to travel linearly down the slot.
- **[08:12]** - **Rotational Mechanics & Arm Trajectories**: Leaders, as you execute the left turn while guiding the follower, strictly manage your arm paths—right arm up, left hand in front of the neck. Keep your core tight to handle the dual rotation, ensuring you do not pull your partner off their established axis.
- **[08:52]** - **Connection Points & Active Resistance**: Establish strict frame integrity. Your arms must remain relaxed but active ("tonic"); never let them hang dead or lock out straight. Both partners must support their own weight, creating a connection based on matched, elastic resistance rather than physical reliance.
- **[09:34]** - **Leader's Axis & Hand Manipulation**: Leaders, control the descent of your left hand during your turn by isolating the arm movement from your rotating torso. You must stay perfectly balanced over your axis to execute the drop catch without disrupting the follower's continuous momentum and timing.
- **[10:10]** - **Spatial Awareness & Drop Catch Execution**: The drop catch behind the neck demands precise spatial awareness. lessons.title: 04 - Spirals
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:45]** - **Weight Transfer & Spiral Mechanics**: The leader demonstrates the foundational spiral step, deliberately placing the heel on count 4. This solid heel strike acts as a crucial anchoring point, allowing for a grounded and controlled rotational weight transfer. The core must remain active to keep the vertical axis aligned over the standing leg during the turn.
- **[01:10]** - **Axis Shifts & Rotational Control**: Notice the explicit weight transfer from the left to the right foot while rotating on the heel. This action requires sharp core isolation and pelvic stability to manage the rotational forces without losing balance. For dancers in heels, the mechanical requirement adapts to a "toe, open" stepping pattern to preserve the center of gravity.
- **[02:10]** - **Footwork Articulation & Syncopation**: Integrating the syncopated rhythm ("7 and 8, 1 and 2") necessitates extremely rapid weight shifts. Dancers must compress into the floor with soft knees to execute these micro-transfers of weight efficiently. Grounding through the balls of the feet ensures the structural integrity of the frame remains unaffected by the fast footwork.
- **[03:45]** - **Core Engagement & Vertical Level Changes**: The sequence introduces subtle vertical level changes ("going up" on counts 3 and 5) combined with lateral movements. This mechanic demands that the core actively manages the center of mass, preventing the upper body from pitch shifting while the lower limbs articulate the directional changes.
- **[08:15]** - **Spatial Awareness in the Cross Body Lead**: Entering the partnerwork phase, the leader opens the slot precisely on counts 5, 6, 7. This spatial management clearly defines the line of dance for the follower. Frame integrity is maintained through lats and back engagement, allowing the leader to invite the follower down the slot without breaking the connection.
- **[08:35]** - **Leader/Follower Mechanics & Grip Transition**: As the follower executes the left turn, the leader guides her rotational axis with a fluid connection. Crucially, on count 1, the leader executes a seamless "palm up" grip change. This micro-articulation maintains a consistent tension/compression cycle, preparing the next rotational sequence without disrupting the flow of energy.
- **[09:40]** - **Torque Generation for Double Outside Turns**: Preparing the follower for a double outside turn, the leader shifts weight to the right on 6 and back on 7. This creates necessary torque and clear directional intent. The leader's core remains tightly engaged to absorb the rotational momentum, providing a stable anchor from which the follower can safely spin.
- **[10:25]** - **Isolation & Safe Connection Points**: The breakdown of the "flick" emphasizes leading from the body rather than the elbow. This vital isolation ensures the frame remains soft and responsive, protecting the follower's shoulder joint from sharp, abrupt forces. The energy transfer relies on core initiation moving through an elastic arm connection.
- **[11:00]** - **Spatial Management & Rotational Axis**: During the follower's double turn, the leader intentionally keeps the guiding arm slightly elevated. This spatial adjustment respects the follower's vertical axis, preventing downward compression that would pull her off balance. It ensures the rotational plane remains clear and unobstructed.
- **[12:25]** - **Tension/Compression & Distance Management**: To arrest the follower's momentum, the leader applies a simultaneous push with the left hand (compression) and pull with the right (tension). The leader actively tracks the follower's spatial trajectory, stepping into the movement to prevent the connection from over-extending, thereby maintaining the structural integrity needed to reverse her direction smoothly.

lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 05 - Suzy Q Variation
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:53]** - **Advanced Suzy Q Variation Initiation**: The sequence begins with a syncopated Suzy Q. Notice the precise weight transfer onto the crossing foot while maintaining a slight bend in the supporting leg. The core must remain engaged to stabilize the upper body against the rapid lateral footwork.
- **[01:46]** - **Weight Transfer & Syncopation Mechanics**: Breaking down the footwork with counts, observe the sharp weight shifts on the syncopated taps. The heel of the standing foot remains grounded to provide stability, while the tapping foot articulates rapidly. The axis of the body shifts dynamically but remains controlled through active core engagement.
- **[03:30]** - **Directional Changes & Axis Shifts**: When executing the variation to the opposite side, the primary challenge is the rapid re-establishment of the vertical axis. The dancer must push off the inside edge of the trailing foot, transferring weight cleanly to the new supporting leg without allowing the upper body to pitch forward or backward.
- **[04:35]** - **Isolations & Arm Styling Integration**: The introduction of arm styling requires a strong dissociation between the upper and lower body. The core acts as the anchor point, allowing the arms to articulate cleanly on the syncopated beats without disrupting the grounding or the rhythm of the footwork below.
- **[06:04]** - **Musicality & Dynamic Weight Control**: Executing the sequence to music highlights the need for dynamic weight control. The dancer must modulate the intensity of their footfalls, using the floor to absorb impact while maintaining a buoyant, active center to stay ahead of the tempo.
- **[08:18]** - **Partnerwork Initiation & Frame Integrity**: The sequence begins with a Cross Body Lead into a double turn. The leader establishes clear rotational intent through a solid frame, utilizing lat engagement rather than arm pulling. The follower must maintain frame tone to receive the torque and translate it into a balanced, on-axis spin.
- **[09:19]** - **Copa Setup & Compression Mechanics**: The transition into the Copa requires precise spatial management. The leader catches the follower's momentum using compression through the connection point, absorbing the energy into his core. The follower must meet this resistance with an active frame, preparing for the redirection of force.
- **[10:13]** - **Spatial Awareness & Continuous Momentum**: During the walk-around and hand change, the leader must manage the distance between partners to maintain connection without crowding the follower's slot. The follower focuses on maintaining her own axis and tracking the leader's center, ensuring a smooth continuation of momentum.
- **[10:53]** - **Follower Mechanics & Prioritizing the Lead**: The follower emphasizes the importance of frame integrity and responsiveness over superficial styling. Styling must be born from the established connection; if the frame drops to execute an arm line, the structural integrity of the partnership fails, and the lead is lost.
- **[12:07]** - **Leader's Axis Adjustment & Spatial Management**: To execute the final turn sequence comfortably, the leader must adjust his body position, utilizing his back and lateral core muscles. Stepping in place rather than forward prevents crowding the follower's slot, maintaining proper spatial distance and allowing the torque to be applied cleanly without pulling the follower off her axis.
- **[13:06]** - **Thoracic Rotation & Connection Points**: The leader details the necessity of thoracic rotation to manage the awkward hand connection during the final turn. By engaging the lats and rotating the upper spine, the leader accommodates the connection without compromising his own balance or restricting the follower's rotational path.
- **[15:15]** - **Full Sequence Execution & Tension/Compression**: Dancing the sequence to music demonstrates the continuous flow of tension and compression between partners. The transitions between the linear Cross Body Leads and the rotational movements rely on instantaneous changes in frame resistance, requiring high levels of core engagement and mutual spatial awareness.

- **[04:00]** - **Directional Shifts and Spatial Awareness**: When executing the half turns, spatial awareness is critical for maintaining the line of dance. - **[09:28]** - **Connection Shift and Momentum Continuance**: The flick behind the back requires a precise and smooth transfer of connection. - **[10:40]** - **Hammerlock Tension and Alignment**: Entering the hammerlock position demands a delicate balance of tension and compression within the frame. - **[00:50]** - **Weight Transfer & Axis Shift**: Initiate the footwork sequence with a slide on counts 6 and 7. Engage your core to drag the foot smoothly without breaking your vertical axis. Transfer your weight precisely on count 1 to ground your body for the subsequent syncopations.
- **[01:04]** - **Foot Articulation & Spatial Awareness**: When executing the double front cross on counts 2 and 3, maintain a tight spatial footprint by keeping your center of gravity directly over the supporting leg. - **[02:00]** - **Heel Swivels & Core Isolation**: Integrate rapid heel-heel, toe-toe swivels by generating significant torque from your hips and core, while keeping your upper body isolated and stable. Keep your weight slightly forward on the balls of your feet to allow your heels to articulate freely without throwing you off balance.
- **[02:55]** - **Rotational Mechanics & Posture**: Incorporate a full right turn initiated by your left shoulder. Brace your core to control the rotational momentum and prevent your axis from tilting. Spotting is crucial here to re-establish your spatial orientation and properly ground your step on count 7.
- **[03:36]** - **Weight Transfer & Leg Isolation**: Introduce a tap on count 8 followed by a double kick on 5, 6. Ensure your supporting leg is perfectly grounded, utilizing micro-adjustments in your ankle and knee to maintain balance. Initiate the kicks from your hip flexor while your core stabilizes the torso.
- **[04:02]** - **Directional Change & Grounding**: During the open step back on 2 and cross over on 4, aggressively drive your weight into the floor to arrest backward momentum and instantly redirect the energy forward. Your core acts as a decelerator, maintaining your frame integrity during this rapid directional change.
- **[05:33]** - **Torso Torquing & Core Engagement**: Enhance the double kick with torso twists. This counter-rotational movement creates a visual dynamic while acting as a counterbalance to your extending leg. Fire your obliques and transverse abdominis aggressively to stabilize your spine during these rapid changes in direction.
- **[07:51]** - **Frame Integrity & Connection Points**: Transition into partnerwork with a foundational Cross Body Lead. As the leader, establish clear connection points through a toned frame, utilizing your lats to guide the follower. As the follower, match this tone, allowing for a seamless translation of energy while maintaining the slot's linear integrity.
- **[08:16]** - **Leader Rotational Mechanics**: Execute the leader's double turn by initiating the rotation from your core while maintaining slight compression in the connection to guide your partner simultaneously. Keep your vertical axis unbroken to complete the rotation smoothly and re-establish your frame on count 5.
- **[09:05]** - **Tension/Compression & Spatial Management**: The wrap/hack maneuver requires precise spatial management. Leaders, guide the follower's arm straight behind your own back, maintaining constant, low-level tension to dictate distance. Followers, stay grounded and responsive, keeping your frame active to absorb and follow the kinetic chain.
- **[10:02]** - **Follower Deceleration & Core Stability**: The leader halts the follower's rotation on count 5, requiring immediate deceleration. Followers, engage your core heavily to arrest momentum without breaking posture or falling off balance. Leaders, use a clear compression block to communicate the stop and manage the kinetic energy.
- **[11:21]** - **Vertical Axis Manipulation & Release**: Exit from the wrap with an "up and down" motion on 5, 6, 7. Leaders, manipulate the follower's vertical axis slightly to create the necessary space for the release. - **[12:05]** - **Follower Spatial Awareness & Distance Management**: Followers, it is crucial to remain in close proximity to the leader during the turning sequences. If you allow the distance to expand, frame integrity is compromised, leading to a loss of connection and control. Actively manage your slot and track the leader's center.
- **[14:06]** - **Shoulder Biomechanics & Frame Safety**: Followers, actively depress your shoulder blade (scapular depression) during turns to protect the rotator cuff and maintain frame stability. chapters.description: Initiate the footwork sequence with a slide on counts 6 and 7. Engage your core to drag the foot smoothly without breaking your vertical axis. Transfer your weight precisely on count 1 to ground your body for the subsequent syncopations.

chapters.title: Foot Articulation & Spatial Awareness
chapters.description: When executing the double front cross on counts 2 and 3, maintain a tight spatial footprint by keeping your center of gravity directly over the supporting leg. Use your ankle and knee joints as shock absorbers to facilitate rapid, isolated foot articulation.

chapters.title: Heel Swivels & Core Isolation
chapters.description: Integrate rapid heel-heel, toe-toe swivels by generating significant torque from your hips and core, while keeping your upper body isolated and stable. chapters.title: Rotational Mechanics & Posture
chapters.description: Incorporate a full right turn initiated by your left shoulder. Brace your core to control the rotational momentum and prevent your axis from tilting. Spotting is crucial here to re-establish your spatial orientation and properly ground your step on count 7.

chapters.title: Weight Transfer & Leg Isolation
chapters.description: Introduce a tap on count 8 followed by a double kick on 5, 6. Ensure your supporting leg is perfectly grounded, utilizing micro-adjustments in your ankle and knee to maintain balance. Initiate the kicks from your hip flexor while your core stabilizes the torso.

chapters.title: Directional Change & Grounding

chapters.title: Torso Torquing & Core Engagement

chapters.title: Frame Integrity & Connection Points
chapters.description: Transition into partnerwork with a foundational Cross Body Lead. chapters.title: Leader Rotational Mechanics
chapters.description: Execute the leader's double turn by initiating the rotation from your core while maintaining slight compression in the connection to guide your partner simultaneously. Keep your vertical axis unbroken to complete the rotation smoothly and re-establish your frame on count 5.

chapters.title: Tension/Compression & Spatial Management
chapters.description: The wrap/hack maneuver requires precise spatial management. Leaders, guide the follower's arm straight behind your own back, maintaining constant, low-level tension to dictate distance. chapters.title: Follower Deceleration & Core Stability

chapters.title: Vertical Axis Manipulation & Release

chapters.title: Follower Spatial Awareness & Distance Management

lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:41]** - **Advanced Shines Introduction & Weight Transfer**: The instructor begins breaking down the advanced shine sequence. Pay close attention to the grounding on each step. The weight transfer must be precise, rolling through the foot to maintain balance during the rapid cross-overs on counts 1, 2, and 3.
- **[01:08]** - **Axis Shift & Spatial Awareness**: Here, the focus is on the syncopated timing, stepping up on 4 and crossing on 5. The axis must shift sharply but with control. The core remains engaged to stabilize the upper body while the lower body executes the open step on 6 and the crossover on 7, managing the spatial footprint tightly within the slot.
- **[01:47]** - **Core Engagement & Foot Articulation**: Introducing the next sequence starting on count 8. The isolation of the lower body is crucial here. The core acts as the anchor, allowing the feet to articulate the step-taps (8, 1, 2) without upper body sway. Grounding through the standing leg provides the necessary stability for these rapid micro-movements.
- **[03:17]** - **Continuous Flow & Axis Control**: Reviewing the full shine sequence slowly. Notice the continuous flow of weight from one foot to the other. The dancer's center of mass stays relatively low and centered, minimizing unnecessary vertical bounce to ensure quick, sharp changes in direction and consistent grounding.
- **[04:35]** - **Bilateral Symmetry & Grounding**: The instructor demonstrates the shine starting on the opposite side. This requires equal core strength and axis control on both sides of the body. The mechanics of the weight transfer remain identical; ensure the stabilizing leg is deeply grounded to absorb the momentum of the crossing steps and maintain posture.
- **[07:44]** - **Partnerwork Introduction & Frame Integrity**: Transitioning into partnerwork, focusing on high-level "loops." The initial basic and cross-body lead establish the baseline frame. The connection must be elastic yet firm, utilizing the lats and core rather than gripping with the hands, establishing the necessary tension to communicate the upcoming rotational forces.
- **[07:51]** - **Loop Mechanics & Spatial Awareness**: Entering the loop sequence (looping on counts 5 and 6). The leader must maintain a high, clear frame. The spatial distance between partners is critical; if the distance is too great, the frame breaks down. The follower must maintain an active frame, responding to the compression through the shoulders and back rather than collapsing the arms.
- **[08:05]** - **Upper Body Isolation & Torque**: A crucial biomechanical detail for the leader during the loops is explained. Instead of just articulating the arms, the leader must move their body back and angle the upper body to create torque. This uses the core to guide the follower's movement, maintaining structural integrity and preventing shoulder strain for both partners.
- **[08:36]** - **Sequential Looping & Connection Points**: Breaking down the specific hand-over-head sequence. The connection points change rapidly, requiring constant micro-adjustments in frame tone. Both partners must keep their axes strictly aligned over their own feet; leaning into the loops will disrupt the shared center of gravity, causing a loss of balance and frame distortion.
- **[09:35]** - **Rotational Mechanics & Grip Articulation**: The transition into the cross-body lead with a loop. The leader alters the grip (palm up, rotate, thumb to the back). This subtle articulation sets up the rotational force for the follower. The leader's core must be pre-engaged to absorb and redirect the follower's forward momentum smoothly down the slot.
- **[10:35]** - **Level Change & Spatial Management**: Executing the cross-body lead where the leader ducks underneath the arm. This requires a rapid level change achieved by softening the knees and hinging slightly at the hips, while keeping the spine long and core active. The leader must clear the slot efficiently to allow the follower to travel linearly without spatial conflict.
- **[11:45]** - **Alternative Connection Points & Compression**: The leader initiates the follower's forward movement on count 1 by connecting at the elbow instead of the hand. This requires a different sensitivity to compression. The follower must offer resistance from the core through the elbow, allowing the leader to lead from their center of mass rather than using isolated arm strength.
- **[12:40]** - **Dynamic Application & Continuous Connection**: Dancing the entire partnerwork sequence to music. Observe how frame integrity and core engagement are maintained throughout the rapid rotational transitions. The leader continuously manages the distance and slot geometry, while the follower responds to the subtle shifts in tension and compression with active following mechanics.

lessons.title: 10 - Twist  Hammerlock
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:41]** - **Leader's Solo Footwork & Axis Shift**: Begin with your solo footwork, establishing a strong, grounded basic step. You must emphasize stepping forward and backward with controlled weight transfers, maintaining a vertical axis directly over your standing leg to prepare your body for the upcoming rotational movements.
- **[00:58]** - **Rotational Core Engagement**: As you initiate the double turn on counts 5, 6, and 7, drive the rotation entirely from your core, not your shoulders. Your feet must articulate cleanly, maintaining constant contact with the floor to ensure stability and balance throughout the rapid spin sequence.
- **[01:31]** - **Foot Articulation in Twists**: During the "double, single, single" twist sequence, focus on continuous weight shifting and precise foot placement. Use the balls of your feet as pivot points; this requires active engagement of your calves and ankles to absorb the rotational forces without compromising your base of support.
- **[03:00]** - **Spatial Awareness & Hook Turn**: When executing the hook turn on count 3, demand precise spatial management of yourself to stay strictly within the slot. Your core must remain incredibly tight to control the rotational momentum, while your hooking leg establishes a tight, centralized vertical axis.
- **[03:21]** - **Continuous Rotational Mechanics**: The instruction to "twist all the time" requires a fluid decoupling of your upper and lower body. Your core acts as the transmission mechanism, absorbing your lower body's twisting action to present a stable, quiet upper body posture, which is essential for clear leading.
- **[05:22]** - **Musicality & Grounding**: As you apply the broken-down footwork to the music, observe how your weight transfers must sync perfectly with the downbeats. Keep your knees consistently soft; this absorbs the impact and allows for instantaneous directional changes while maintaining an unshakable connection to the floor.
- **[07:41]** - **Initiating the Hammerlock**: Moving into partnerwork, initiate the hammerlock by raising your right hand while keeping the left hand low. Frame integrity is paramount here; you must use back and lat engagement to lead the follower into rotation, ensuring you do not pull or yank with your distal extremities (arms).
- **[08:21]** - **Leader/Follower Tension in Open Break**: As you transition into the synchronized twist section, open the follower up to create a defined stretch across the connection. Both partners must maintain a slight backward pitch from the center, using active compression and tension to stay connected while executing independent, counter-balancing twists.
- **[08:52]** - **Preparation & Spatial Management**: When prepping the follower on count 1, execute a definitive weight shift and an engaged frame to broadcast the upcoming rotation. You must manage the spatial distance meticulously to provide the follower with adequate room to turn without collapsing the structural integrity of the connection.
- **[09:18]** - **Frame Integrity & Rotational Control**: Pay close attention to count 6: use your knuckles to create subtle tension against the follower's hand, actively preventing her from overturning. This is a crucial application of frame integrity—using physical resistance rather than pulling force to guide her momentum and arrest the rotation precisely.
- **[10:52]** - **Hand Connection & Fine Motor Control**: During the hand toss and catch, elevate your left thumb and initiate the catch using your pinky finger. This requires advanced fine motor control and a relaxed yet highly responsive frame. Keep the connection light to facilitate a fluid transition without jarring the follower's established axis.
- **[12:20]** - **Axis Shifting for Final Spins**: To prepare for the final double turn, step in on count 1 to instantly close the spatial distance. This allows the follower to establish her axis perfectly vertical over her standing leg; this close proximity is required to give her the centripetal stability needed for rapid consecutive spins.
- **[13:04]** - **Follower Mechanics & Independent Axis**: Followers, when released from the hammerlock, you must execute the subsequent turn completely independently. Engage your core immediately upon release to maintain your own rotational momentum and vertical axis; do not rely on the leader's frame to salvage your balance.
- **[13:37]** - **Full Sequence Execution & Dynamic Connection**: Dancing the complete pattern to music requires a constant, micro-recalibration of tension and compression. Both partners must maintain fiercely engaged cores and active frames, ensuring seamless biomechanical communication and precise spatial awareness through every complex turn and twist.

chapters.title: Weight Transfer & Axis Shift
chapters.description: Adolfo introduces the shines sequence starting with a Susy Q. Notice the precise articulation of the feet; the weight is maintained primarily on the balls of the feet, allowing for rapid direction changes while keeping the center of gravity stable and the vertical axis aligned.

chapters.title: Grounding Mechanics
chapters.description: On count 7, the weight drops securely onto the right foot. This grounding action is crucial as it establishes a solid base of support. The left leg opens with only the ball of the foot making contact, creating visual extension without compromising the established balance.

chapters.title: Core Engagement for Rotational Force
chapters.description: The twist outward on count 7 requires sharp core engagement. The rotation must be initiated from the obliques and hips rather than just the feet, ensuring the upper body remains quiet while the lower body generates dynamic torque.

chapters.title: Momentum Management
chapters.description: When reversing direction and coming back, the weight transfer must be clean and deliberate. The shift from the right foot stepping out to the left foot stepping down requires a controlled deceleration of momentum, managed by an engaged core and soft, shock-absorbing knees.

chapters.title: Syncopated Foot Articulation
chapters.description: The sequence of taps and heel strikes (counts 8, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) demands extreme ankle mobility and precise weight distribution. The supporting leg must remain softly bent to absorb the impact of the rapid taps while maintaining continuous grounding into the floor.

chapters.title: Lower Body Isolation & Stability
chapters.description: The "in, out, in, out" movement of the left foot (counts 8 through 5) is a masterclass in lower body isolation. The weight stays entirely on the supporting right leg, which acts as a stabilizing pillar, while the active leg articulates freely from the hip joint down to the foot.

chapters.title: Bilateral Core Stability
chapters.description: Practicing the sequence on the opposite side highlights the necessity for balanced biomechanics. Ensure the weight transfers and axis shifts mirror the original side exactly, demanding the same level of core stability and consistent ground pressure.

chapters.title: Frame Integrity in Closed Connection
chapters.description: Transitioning into the partnerwork, the initial connection is established with the leader's right hand securely placed on the follower's shoulder blade. This creates a solid point of compression, allowing for clear communication of intention without the need to grip or pull with the fingers.

chapters.title: Spatial Awareness in the Wrap
chapters.description: As the follower is wrapped, the leader's hand remains fixed on the shoulder blade, avoiding any sliding to maintain consistent tension. The completion of the movement leaves both partners sideways, requiring strict spatial awareness to respect the slot and prepare for the next directional change.

chapters.title: Tension, Release, and Slot Management
chapters.description: The leader initiates the next turn by pulling slightly with the right arm, creating a clear line of tension. As the follower's arm travels over, the leader moves underneath, utilizing precise spatial awareness to clear the follower's path while maintaining a fluid, unbroken physical connection.

chapters.title: Pre-Lead and Frame Resistance
chapters.description: For the turn on counts 6 and 7, the leader must provide a clear pre-lead. The follower needs to feel the structural resistance from the leader's frame to know exactly when to engage their core for the rotation. The persistent placement of the leader's arm on the shoulder blade serves as the biomechanical cue for the follower to keep their arm over.

chapters.title: Axis Maintenance During Double Turns
chapters.description: Leading a double turn requires perfect vertical axis alignment from both partners. The leader must guide the rotational force squarely over the follower's center of gravity. The follower must engage their core tightly to prevent any wobbling or deviation from their spinning axis.

chapters.title: Compression and Directional Control
chapters.description: During the enchufla variation, the leader's right hand (palm down) provides downward compression, guiding the follower forward on counts 2 and 3. The leader then steps in place, absorbing the generated energy and redirecting the momentum firmly downwards on 5, 6, 7 to prep the follower's weight for the subsequent opening.

chapters.title: Managing Rotational Energy and Centrifugal Force
chapters.description: When leading continuous turns, the leader's hands remain elevated, signaling the continuation of rotation. The leader must calibrate their lead to match the follower's natural turning speed, providing structural support without rushing the movement; forcing the speed will cause the follower to lose centrifugal control and balance.

lessons.legacyPath: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced/12 - Combinations working on Syncopations  Turns.mp4
lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 12 - Combinations working on Syncopations  Turns
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:50]** - **Weight Transfer & Axis Shift in Basic Step**: Observe the precise weight transfer on the ball of the foot during the fundamental basic step. The axis shifts smoothly over the standing leg, maintaining a soft knee for continuous grounding and readiness for rapid directional changes.
- **[00:58]** - **Core Engagement in Spiral Turn**: Initiation of the spiral turn requires the core to be fully engaged to maintain strict vertical alignment. The rotational torque is generated from the floor up, with the upper body following the hips, ensuring a tight, balanced rotation without traveling off-axis.
- **[01:10]** - **Foot Articulation in Syncopation**: Introduction of the syncopated footwork sequence. This demands rapid, precise foot articulation where the weight must stay aggressively forward over the toes. This posture allows for quick, rebounding directional changes without the heel striking heavily and disrupting the center of gravity.
- **[01:55]** - **Spatial Awareness in Crossing Steps**: During the intricate crossing steps, notice how the spatial distance is strictly managed. The crossing foot is placed precisely without over-committing the weight, which would pull the dancer off their vertical axis and disrupt the inherent line of dance.
- **[03:10]** - **Balance and Isolation in Tap Sequences**: When executing the tapping sequences, the standing leg must remain perfectly grounded and static. The tapping leg is isolated, moving independently without shifting the primary axis, demonstrating high-level core stability and lower-body control.
- **[04:09]** - **Rotational Forces in Multi-Turns**: When executing multiple turns, maintaining a tight rotational axis is paramount. The rotational force is preserved by keeping the arms compressed close to the body, reducing the moment of inertia, while the core remains rigidly engaged to prevent off-axis wobbling or deceleration.
- **[05:21]** - **Grounding Dynamics with Musical Rhythm**: Integrating the complex solo footwork with music demands an intensified focus on grounding. The dancer must actively push into the floor, using the resulting compression to accelerate through the syncopations and accurately accent the musical hits without floating.
- **[07:44]** - **Frame Integrity in Partnerwork Initiation**: Transitioning to partnerwork, the leader establishes an active frame immediately, utilizing the lats and core rather than solely relying on arm strength to communicate the lead. The follower responds with matched muscular tone, creating a solid, reliable connection point for energy transfer.
- **[08:00]** - **Torque and Compression in Hand Tosses**: The execution of the behind-the-neck pull and toss requires precise torque generation from the leader's core. The follower must maintain frame resistance to receive this kinetic energy safely, preventing a collapse of the connection and allowing for a smooth redirection of momentum.
- **[08:16]** - **Spatial Management in Intricate Arm Styling**: Guiding the follower's arm into a locked position behind the neck requires acute spatial awareness. The distance between partners must be meticulously managed to allow the arm to pass smoothly without over-rotating the shoulder joint or breaking the follower's posture.
- **[09:07]** - **Leader/Follower Mechanics in Hand Flicks**: The leader initiates a subtle hand flick, a complex lead requiring high tactile sensitivity. The follower's frame must be adequately responsive to catch this quick impulse and translate it into the intended rotational styling movement without losing the primary rhythm or structural alignment.
- **[10:19]** - **Counterbalance and Tension in Double Arm Drops**: During the double arm drop and redirection, both partners must firmly engage their cores to create a functional counterbalance. This shared tension allows for a spring-like kinetic reaction, absorbing the downward force and smoothly propelling them into the subsequent rotational sequence.
- **[11:28]** - **Rotational Control and Compression in Copa Entry**: Entering the Copa (in-and-out) mechanism, the leader uses targeted compression to arrest the follower's forward momentum, followed immediately by tension to redirect her. The follower must maintain a rigid vertical axis and utilize the frame connection to control her rotational speed and trajectory.
- **[12:17]** - **Fluidity and Isolation in Hammerlock Transitions**: When transitioning into the hammerlock position, the leader must guide the follower smoothly, ensuring her rotational path is clear so the arm is not torqued uncomfortably. The follower must isolate her shoulder joint, permitting the necessary rotation while keeping her core square to her primary vertical axis.
- **[13:27]** - **Dynamic Frame Maintenance at Tempo**: Executing the full partnerwork combination to tempo reveals the necessity of dynamic frame mechanics. The structural integrity, weight transfer, and active connection must be rigidly maintained despite the increased rotational speed, with core engagement acting as the central anchor for both partners.

lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 13 - Palladium  Partnerwork Combination
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[01:00]** - **Weight Transfer & Axis Control**: The sequence begins with a deliberate manipulation of the basic step timing, stepping on count 1, holding count 2, and executing rapid weight transfers on 3, 4, and 5. This requires acute core engagement to stabilize the axis during the syncopation, ensuring the weight is fully committed to the stepping foot before the next rapid transition.
- **[01:46]** - **Core Engagement & Isolation**: During the kick on count 1, the core must be tightly engaged to maintain balance and prevent the upper body from pitching forward or backward. The subsequent double tap on counts 6 and 7 demands precise isolation of the lower body, using the standing leg's slight flexion to absorb the impact while keeping the torso quiet.
- **[02:30]** - **Weight Transfer & Grounding**: When executing the weight shift forward on count 1 and tapping on count 2, focus on grounding through the supporting leg. The center of mass moves forward, but the hips remain tucked under the shoulders to maintain a strong vertical axis, allowing for a seamless transition into the following basic step.
- **[03:26]** - **Spatial Awareness & Axis Recalibration**: The instructor introduces a timing shift, initiating the basic with a forward step on count 6. This challenges the dancer's internal metronome and spatial awareness. You must recalibrate your axis and line of dance to accommodate the reversed weight transfer pattern without losing the rhythmic pocket.
- **[04:02]** - **Weight Transfer & Momentum Control**: To return to standard timing, the dancer steps back on 1 and taps on 2. This requires a sudden deceleration and reversal of momentum. The core acts as the primary braking system here, arresting the backward travel and stabilizing the axis before the weight is fully transferred back to the forward foot on count 3.
- **[08:05]** - **Frame Integrity & Leader Mechanics**: Entering the double turn hammerlock via the cross body lead, the leader must establish a firm but elastic frame. The initiation comes from the leader's core rotating and sending energy down the arm, not from pulling with the bicep. The connection point must remain consistent to guide the follower securely through the rotation without collapsing the spatial distance.
- **[08:42]** - **Spatial Awareness & Torque Application**: As the leader takes the follower's left arm over, precise spatial management is critical. The leader must create enough clearance for the follower's axis while applying subtle torque to encourage the continued rotation. Releasing the left hand precisely on time allows the follower's momentum to carry her through the extra turn smoothly.
- **[09:27]** - **Frame Integrity & Connection Mechanics**: During the follower's subsequent double turn, the leader's right arm must maintain structural integrity, acting as a fixed pivot point. The instruction to keep the arm straight and the palm down ensures the connection remains at the follower's natural rotation level, preventing the frame from breaking upward and destabilizing her axis.
- **[10:20]** - **Leader/Follower Mechanics & Tactile Communication**: Following the release, the slide down the follower's arm to re-establish the handhold demonstrates advanced connection mechanics. This slide maintains continuous, soft tactile communication, allowing both partners to read each other's momentum and intention without abruptly jarring the frame or losing the established tension.
- **[11:08]** - **Spatial Awareness & Dynamic Catching**: The drop catch maneuver requires impeccable timing and spatial calibration. The leader must accurately predict the trajectory of the follower's hand post-turn to execute the catch seamlessly. The core must be braced to absorb any residual rotational energy as the connection is re-established, grounding both partners instantly.
- **[12:16]** - **Core Engagement & Rotational Counterbalance**: During the loop over the head and the leader's subsequent turn, both partners must maintain active cores. The leader's turn is initiated by a sharp rotation of the hips and torso, while the follower maintains frame resistance to provide a stable counterbalance. This shared dynamic allows for rapid, controlled rotational changes within the slot.

lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 14 - Angle Double kick  Partnerwork Combinations
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:52]** - **Weight Transfer & Axis Shift**: Initiation of the solo footwork (shines). The instructor emphasizes a grounded basic step. Notice how the weight transfers smoothly through the metatarsals to the heel, keeping the center of gravity low and stable before initiating the angular changes.
- **[01:05]** - **Spatial Awareness & Core Engagement**: The transition into the diagonal line. The core must be fully engaged to arrest the forward momentum on count 4, redirecting the body's energy for the sequence starting on count 5. This requires precise spatial awareness to maintain the slot.
- **[01:13]** - **Foot Articulation & Balance**: Demonstration of the "Double Kick". This movement requires significant core stability and an isolated, grounded supporting leg. The ankle and knee articulate sharply while the upper body remains entirely quiet, demonstrating advanced isolation.
- **[01:30]** - **Directional Change & Momentum Control**: Crossing on count 5 requires a sharp pivot. The axis must be perfectly aligned over the supporting foot to allow for a quick change of direction without losing balance or falling out of the rhythm.
- **[01:56]** - **Hook & Mambo Jazz Mechanics**: The hook action demands external rotation of the hip and a quick weight transfer. The subsequent 'Mambo Jazz' step utilizes a contra-body motion, where the torso twists in opposition to the lower body, relying on oblique engagement for torque.
- **[02:44]** - **Syncopated Weight Transfer**: Breakdown of the fast, syncopated rhythm. This section requires micro-weight transfers. Instead of fully committing weight to the floor, the dancer uses the balls of the feet to quickly rebound, keeping the center of gravity slightly elevated but controlled by the core.
- **[04:36]** - **Upper Body Isolation & Tone**: The instructor highlights the specific shoulder and torso motion during the syncopation. The latissimus dorsi and obliques are engaged to create a sharp, controlled contraction, rather than letting the arms flail. This isolation adds texture to the footwork.
- **[08:10]** - **Leader Initiation & Frame Integrity**: Transitioning to partnerwork with a Cross Body Lead. The leader opens the slot by shifting their axis back and to the left, creating a clear pathway. The frame remains toned, using the back muscles to invite the follower forward without pulling with the arms.
- **[08:38]** - **Rotational Torque & Connection Points**: Executing the reverse turn for the follower. The leader establishes a clear connection point, applying subtle rotational pressure (torque) through the fingers and wrist. The follower maintains an engaged core to translate this pressure into a controlled pivot on their axis.
- **[08:44]** - **Spatial Awareness & Axis Management**: The leader's turn. The leader must spot their partner while managing their own rotational axis. The footwork allows the leader to stay tight within the slot, avoiding encroachment on the follower's space while maintaining visual connection.
- **[09:25]** - **Tension & Compression in Closed Hold**: Re-establishing the closed frame. Notice the immediate restoration of tone. The leader's right hand on the follower's shoulder blade and the follower's left arm resting with slight downward pressure create a cohesive unit ready for the next directional change.
- **[09:44]** - **Redirection & Resistance**: The shoulder catch. The leader arrests the follower's forward momentum by presenting a firm, unyielding frame at the shoulder. The follower must meet this resistance by engaging their core and absorbing the energy through a soft supporting knee, preparing to be redirected.
- **[10:12]** - **Vertical Displacement & Elasticity**: The vertical arm motion. While the arms move through a large vertical range, the connection remains elastic. The leader maintains a constant, slight tension, ensuring the follower can track the movement without losing the rhythmic pulse or vertical balance.
- **[11:00]** - **Distance Management & Looped Turns**: Passing the hand over the head. The leader must manage the spatial distance perfectly—too close, and the turn is cramped; too far, and the connection breaks. The follower maintains a consistent step size, trusting the leader's frame to guide the rotation.
- **[11:52]** - **Compression in the Copa**: The Copa (In and Out) requires a distinct preparation. The leader creates compression by absorbing the follower's momentum into their right hand and core. The follower matches this compression, creating a "spring-loaded" effect that propels them into the subsequent rotation.
- **[12:05]** - **Micro-Connection & Finger Lead**: The instructor demonstrates stopping the follower using just two fingers. This highlights extreme frame efficiency; it relies entirely on the follower's sensitivity to structural resistance and core engagement, proving that leading is about body mechanics, not grip strength.
- **[12:12]** - **Torso Rotation & Neck Connection**: Placing the arm behind the neck. The leader uses the connection at the neck to guide the follower's upper body rotation. The follower must maintain cervical spine alignment and allow the torque to travel down through their core to initiate the lower body turn.

lessons.title: 15 - Pachanga I
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:47]** - **Weight Transfer & Pachanga Foundation**: The instructor introduces the fundamental Pachanga rhythm, emphasizing a continuous, grounded bounce. Weight must remain primarily on the balls of the feet with a soft, active knee bend to allow for rapid weight shifts and swiveling actions without compromising the vertical axis.
- **[01:14]** - **Core Engagement & Swivel Mechanics**: Transitioning from a foundational basic into the Pachanga swivels. The core must remain tightly engaged to isolate the lower body rotation from the upper body frame. The swiveling action is generated from the hips and knees, driving into the floor, while the shoulders remain relatively square to the line of dance.
- **[01:31]** - **Syncopated Weight Shifts & Grounding**: Introduction of syncopated footwork. Maintaining grounding is critical here; the rapid weight transfers require the dancer to push down into the floor rather than lifting up. The center of mass must stay low and controlled to execute the quick, syncopated rhythms cleanly.
- **[02:01]** - **Axis Shifting & Kick Variations**: Incorporating kicks into the swivel framework. lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 16 - Tumbao Steps  Turn Partnerwork
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[01:00]** - **Weight Transfer in Tumbao Footwork**: The instructor introduces the foundational tap-step mechanism. Notice the emphasis on a singular, fluid motion rather than a disjointed tap followed by a step. This requires keeping the knees soft and articulating through the metatarsals to ensure a smooth transition of the center of mass without bouncing.
- **[02:00]** - **Axis Control in Suzie Q**: A detailed breakdown of the Suzie Q weight shift. The focus here is on maintaining a centralized axis. Instead of transferring weight entirely left and right, the dancer utilizes a single, grounded motion, requiring significant core engagement to stabilize the upper body while the lower body crosses the midline.
- **[02:59]** - **Frame Integrity in Solo Holds**: During the open breaks of the footwork sequence, the instructor emphasizes "holding" the position. This is achieved by engaging the latissimus dorsi and core, creating a structural tonality in the arms and torso even without a partner. This internal resistance preps the body for sudden directional changes and maintains aesthetic lines.
- **[04:03]** - **Syncopated Foot Articulation**: The sequence introduces a syncopated "cha-cha" rhythm. Execution of these rapid weight changes requires precise foot articulation and keeping the center of gravity relatively low. The grounding allows for quick, controlled bursts of movement without compromising balance or rushing the musical phrasing.
- **[08:18]** - **Follower Frame and Connection Tonality**: Transitioning into partnerwork, the follower emphasizes an active but light frame. The connection should not rely on downward pressure or "heaviness." Instead, both partners must maintain their own axis and core stability, meeting at the connection point with matched, responsive resistance to facilitate seamless communication.
- **[08:52]** - **Leader Initiation and Timing Mechanics**: For the follower's double turn, the leader initiates the rotational force exactly on count 1. This precise timing is crucial as it dictates the follower's momentum, giving her the required time to step securely and ground her axis on count 2. The initiation comes from a grounded rotation of the leader's core, transferred through a stable frame.
- **[09:40]** - **Follower Spatial Awareness and Axis Shifts**: During the leader's left turn, the follower must acutely manage her spatial footprint. By stepping the 6 in place and executing a tight left turn, she respects the linear slot. The subsequent forward step requires a clear, committed axis shift, driven by a controlled push from the standing leg.
- **[10:48]** - **Frame Integrity and the "Block" Mechanism**: The leader establishes a physical boundary or "block" on the follower's right side to execute the back-spot turn. This connection point must be solid enough to arrest her forward momentum. The leader achieves this by anchoring the connection to his core and lats, ensuring his arm does not collapse under the follower's kinetic energy.
- **[11:29]** - **Biomechanical Redirection and Momentum Control**: A deeper analysis of the "block" execution. If the leader allows the follower to travel forward before applying resistance, the structural integrity of the frame fails. The lock must be established simultaneously with her forward step on 1, instantly converting her linear momentum into rotational energy around a shared central axis.
- **[12:10]** - **Follower Spatial Orientation and Styling**: The follower targets a specific spatial orientation (3 o'clock) on count 6. This deliberate spotting prepares her cervical spine for the upcoming rotation. The immediate engagement of the right arm requires an isolation of the shoulder girdle, keeping the movement strictly stylistic without destabilizing her core engagement.
- **[12:50]** - **Spatial Management in Rapid Weight Shifts**: Due to the compressed timing of the pattern, the open break must be spatially conservative. The leader minimizes his linear travel, relying on a subtle, deeply grounded weight shift to lead the movement. The follower reciprocates by utilizing core isolation to absorb the directional change quickly, enabling her to step back onto the left foot without over-committing her center of gravity.

lessons.course: Adolfo Indacochea  Tania Cannarsa - Salsa On2 Advanced
lessons.title: 17 - Pachanga II
lessons.rawSummary:
- **[00:50]** - **Pachanga Footwork Initiation & Weight Transfer**: Observe the initiation of the Pachanga basic. The weight transfers are meticulously controlled, utilizing the ball of the foot to establish grounding. The core must remain engaged to isolate the lower body mechanics, ensuring the upper body remains quiet while the feet articulate the syncopated rhythms.
- **[01:21]** - **Axis Shifts & Swivel Mechanics**: During the transition to the swivel taps on counts 6, 7, 8, 1, the dancer must actively manage their center of gravity. The weight shifts require a soft knee to absorb the impact and maintain a continuous flow. The axis shifts laterally, demanding strong core engagement to prevent overbalancing.
- **[01:43]** - **Level Changes & Core Stability**: As the sequence incorporates a drop on count 1, the compression into the floor is paramount. The descent must be controlled by the quads and glutes, not just gravity. The core acts as a stabilizing pillar, allowing the upper body to maintain posture while the lower body executes the level change.
- **[02:16]** - **Grounding Through Hop Transitions**: Notice the subtle hops integrated into the footwork. Grounding is critical here; the dancer must land with a bent knee to absorb the kinetic energy. The spatial awareness of the foot placement ensures the base of support remains directly underneath the center of mass, preventing any loss of equilibrium.
- **[03:25]** - **Syncopated Weight Transfers & Isolation**: In this advanced variation, the weight transfers are rapid and syncopated (3 and 4, 5 and 6). The isolation of the hips is crucial, allowing the feet to articulate independently of the torso. Frame integrity, even without a partner, is maintained through lat engagement to keep the arms stable and counterbalance the dynamic footwork.
- **[07:43]** - **Frame Integrity During Hand Toss**: Transitioning into partnerwork, observe the Cross Body Lead with a hand toss. The leader establishes connection and resistance before the toss. The follower must maintain an active frame, engaging the lats to ensure the arm doesn't collapse when re-establishing connection, allowing for a seamless transfer of rotational energy.
- **[08:00]** - **Leader Mechanics & Rotational Torque**: The leader utilizes their body mechanics, specifically moving the shoulders forward sequentially, to generate rotational torque for the follower's turn. This is not driven by pulling the arm, but by shifting the center of mass and using frame compression to guide the follower through her slot.
- **[09:00]** - **Spatial Awareness & Pacing the Turn**: A critical breakdown of leading the follower's turn. The leader must control the pace, allowing the follower to step through her axis on the 1, 2, 3 rather than spinning her off-balance. This requires acute spatial awareness and an elongated frame connection to guide her through the rotation smoothly.
- **[10:19]** - **Compression & Blocking the Follower**: The leader creates a physical block on count 3 by stepping in place and establishing compression through the connection point. This resistance signals the follower to halt her forward momentum. The core must be highly engaged by both partners to absorb and respond to this sudden change in dynamic energy.
- **[10:48]** - **Creating Resistance for Leader's Turn**: To execute the leader's turn into the hammerlock, the leader utilizes the established compression on count 3 to propel themselves into the rotation on 5. The frame remains structured, using the connection to the follower as a pivot point. The follower provides counter-resistance to maintain the tension necessary for the leader's rotation.
- **[11:46]** - **Multi-Axial Hand Manipulation & Follower Response**: The leader guides the follower forward while manipulating the arms in a multi-axial pattern (down and up). The follower must maintain a hyper-responsive frame, keeping constant tension in the arms to interpret the complex directional changes without losing her structural integrity or linear trajectory.
- **[12:03]** - **Release & Spatial Realignment**: The sequence concludes with a dual hand flick release. The energy is sent outward, and both partners must immediately re-engage their core to stabilize their individual axes. Spatial awareness is critical as they exit the rotation and realign within the line of dance for the next basic step.

This demands precise isolation of the lower leg from the knee down, keeping the upper thigh and hip stable. The core must be fully engaged to control the momentum and prevent lateral swaying during these fast, off-axis foot placements.
- **[02:58]** - **Spatial Awareness & Directional Changes**: Executing the half-turn pivot within the shine sequence.
